newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Kabila, Mobutu agree to meet, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila, Mobutu agree to meet, U.S. says.

text.p: U.S. troubleshooter Bill Richardson said on Tuesday rebel leader Laurent Kabila and President Mobutu Sese Seko had agreed to a first face-to-face meeting.

"The objective of President (Bill) Clinton sending me here is to have face-to-face talks between President Mobutu and President Kabila," Richardson said on arrival in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi from the capital Kinshasa to meet Kabila.

"I am happy that both men have agreed to meet. But I will be working out other details with Mr Kabila on free and fair elections, the rule of law which should follow after the end of the war in Zaire," said Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations.

"I had a very fruitful meeting with President Mobutu on the general situation in Zaire, which as you all know is at war," he said. Richardson had 90 minutes of talks with Mobutu earlier on Tuesday and said a good goal for the meeting would be this weekend.
His initial reference to Kabila as president apparently was aimed at driving home a U.S. point that Mobutu should step down.

Before Richardson arrived in Lubumbashi, Kabila told Reuters: "I have agreed to (South African) President (Nelson) Mandela's request that I meet Mr Mobutu on a ship off the Atlantic coastline to discuss Mr Mobutu's departure."
He said the ship would be a South African navy vessel off the coast of Zaire.
"As far as I am concerned this will be a short ceremony at which Mr Mobutu is supposed to agree to leave, otherwise our forces now advancing on the route to Kinshasa will eject him.
"I am made to believe he (Mobutu) will cooprate with us and avoid a bloody confrontation for Kinshasa," Kabila added.

Asked about when, Kabila said it would be in the next few days and Mandela and U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun were working on an agreeable date but the most important thing was that both men had agreed to meet.
Kabila announced his agreement to a meeting shortly after his rebels entered the town of Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from Kinshasa, and were greeted by crowds of jubilant residents.
He said talks would go hand-in-hand with a rebel offensive and said rebel forces were now advancing towards Kinshasa from Kikwit after seizing the town and its airport on Tuesday.

In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said it had "increasingly shocking reports" of killings of refugees around Kisangani and other areas of eastern Zaire held by the rebels and demanded a full investigation.
South Africa said earlier on Tuesday talks between the two war foes, chaired by Mandela, were imminent but gave no venue.
Mobutu, who has cancer, ruled out South Africa as too far on health grounds. Kabila ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, and Gabon on security grounds.
South Africa's Business Day newspaper said the South African naval supply ship Outeniqua could host talks in international waters off Zaire or Angola's neighbouring Cabinda enclave.
A senior rebel commander said in Lubumbashi that Mobutu's Presidential Guard had strongly defended Kikwit airport, which rebels needed as a springboard for a final assault on Kinshasa.
Richardson plans to visit Zaire's rebel-held third city of Kisangani on Wednesday and possibly Angola, which Kinshasa has accused of invading Zaire to back the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
The rebels, fighting since October, control over half of Zaire, Africa's third largest nation at the continent's heart.
Richardson's trip to Kisangani will focus on the plight of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans.
The rebels have been accused of driving the Hutu refugees into the jungle in the hope that they will die there. Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days to repatriate them to Rwanda.

"We are receiving increasingly shocking reports of killings of refugees both in the area around Kisangani and elsewhere," Pamela O'Toole, U.N. refugee agency spokeswoman. "These killings must stop and an urgent investigation must be launched."
U.N. agencies managed to send some aid on Tuesday to thousands of Rwandan refugees emerging from hiding in forests south of Kisangai but had problems with rebel cooperation.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
